articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation, Modifying Listing for Volta Shipping Services LLC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an update to its Iran sanctions program on November 9, 2026. This action modifies the listing for VOLTA SHIPPING SERVICES LLC, also known as VOLTA SHIPPING SERVICES FZCO.

The entity's alias has been changed to VOLTA CONTAINER LINE FZCO, while its address, establishment dates, licenses, and registration numbers remain consistent. The designation continues to carry a secondary sanctions risk under Section 2 of Executive Order 13902 and is linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani.

This update is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the accuracy and effectiveness of its sanctions lists, ensuring that entities involved in prohibited activities related to Iran are correctly identified.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canadian Money Services Businesses for Facilitating Iranian Sanctions Evasion
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight Canada-based money services businesses (MSBs) on November 6, 2026, for their alleged role in operating within the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. This action was taken as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' under Executive Order 13902.

These MSBs are accused of facilitating the exchange of Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, thereby enabling international transactions involving Iran and bypassing existing sanctions. Many of the designated businesses reportedly engaged with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The designated entities include 1380079 BC LTD (a.k.a. AMIN EXCHANGE VANCOUVER), 2397639 ONTARIO LTD (a.k.a. FARAH EXCHANGE), B GALAXY INC (a.k.a. C EXCHANEG), and NIA NATIONS CURRENCY LTD (a.k.a. NIA EXCHANGE), among others. OFAC coordinated this action with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Canada's financial intelligence unit (FINTRAC), and the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Cyber, Transnational Crime, and Cuban Sectors; Publishes Cuba-Related Determination
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related activities, transnational criminal organizations, and entities within Cuba. OFAC also published a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically targeting the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy.'

The designations include individuals and entities linked to global scam networks and their enabling corporate infrastructure. Among those added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List are individuals such as CHUI, Kok Wa (Malaysia), HE, Yujing (China/Vanuatu), PANG, Visal (Cambodia/China), and QIU, Yong (Cambodia/Turkey/Saint Lucia), all linked to transnational criminal organizations like the Prince Group.

Additionally, EMPRESA COMERCIALIZADORA DE SERVICIOS TECNICOS Y TECNOLOGICOS (a.k.a. TECNOSIME) in Havana, Cuba, a state-owned enterprise in the petroleum and natural gas extraction support sector, was designated under the Cuba sanctions program. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial activities and support for the Cuban regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, targeting a network accused of providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's 'shadow fleet.' This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and aims to disrupt Iran's sanctions-evasion, aviation, and military procurement networks.

OFAC sanctioned 13 individuals and companies, including an India-based network led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, for their involvement in facilitating Iranian petroleum shipments. Concurrently, OFAC issued an alert warning against the use of false flags by Iran's shadow fleet.

In a separate but related action, OFAC also issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, authorizing certain transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond on or after December 18, 2026, replacing General License 5Z, and amended FAQ 595 to reflect this update.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of International Development Bank for Investment and Finance
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

This amended general license provides a limited authorization for activities ordinarily incident and necessary to conclude business with the specified entity. Such actions are crucial for ensuring an orderly cessation of transactions while maintaining compliance with U.S. sanctions.
The issuance of General License FF-1 reflects OFAC's ongoing management of its sanctions programs, allowing for specific, time-limited activities to mitigate unintended consequences of designations.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Facilitators of DPRK IT Worker Fraud and Supporters of M23 in DRC
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and an entity involved in North Korean IT worker fraud schemes and those supporting the M23 group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The North Korea-related designations include individuals like Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov, Han Yu Song, and Ri Thae Chol, along with the entity First Financial and Technical Development Center, for their roles in generating revenue for North Korea's weapons programs through fraudulent identities and cryptocurrency transfers.

Separately, OFAC also sanctioned the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and a financial institution for their alleged support of the M23 rebel group, which has been destabilizing eastern DRC. These actions underscore the U.S. commitment to countering illicit activities and promoting stability in these regions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by the designated entity JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, citing reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and substantial harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives. A parallel non-prosecution agreement was reached with the Department of Justice, with a portion of the OFAC settlement deemed satisfied by payments under that agreement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 26, 2026, that it is amending several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of an ongoing review to ensure that published guidance remains current.

The amended FAQs, specifically numbers 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, provide clarifications on various aspects of sanctions compliance. These include guidance on jurisdictions subject to broad sanctions, procedures for blocking accounts and funds transfers, interest requirements on blocked funds, and when to reject versus block a transaction.

The revisions also address notification requirements for customers when property is blocked, handling of account openings and transactions involving blocked persons, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions. These updates aim to enhance clarity and assist U.S. persons in fulfilling their compliance obligations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Amends FAQs
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations. Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related actions include the issuance of Iran General License GG, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Karnakis and Karnakis,' and Iran General License HH, 'Authorizing Wind Down Activities, Limited Safety and Environmental Transactions, and the Offloading of Cargo Involving Certain Persons or Vessels Blocked on October 21, 2026.'

For Russia, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions for the Negotiation of and Entry Into Contingent Contracts for the Sale of Lukoil International GmbH and Related Maintenance Activities.' The agency also updated FAQs 1224 and 1225 and made changes to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses Targeting Chinese Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, adding several Chinese entities to its Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List. These actions aim to counter threats to American intellectual property.

Among the designated entities are BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I), BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE II VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND II), and BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN ZHIYUAN ENTERPRISE MANAGEMENT CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP. These entities face blocking of property and restrictions on loans and foreign exchange transactions.

Concurrently, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.

The violations involved nine instances of exporting networking equipment and related services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by a designated entity.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, highlighting the importance of thorough due diligence, especially when dealing with entities in high-risk jurisdictions or those with complex ownership structures.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 10, 2027
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has further extended the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This rule, formally titled 'Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities,' was initially set to take effect on November 10, 2026.

The Affiliates Rule, if implemented, would significantly expand export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned 50 percent or more, directly or indirectly, by parties on the BIS Entity List, Military End-User (MEU) List, or certain Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs).

This extension provides companies with additional time to prepare for the expanded customer due diligence burdens that the rule would impose. The ongoing suspension is reportedly linked to broader U.S.-China trade negotiations, suggesting that the ultimate effective date or form of the rule may depend on the outcome of these discussions.

articles.headline: Commerce Department Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms, easing compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
